resident.chief_complaint: Progressive unsteadiness and bilateral lower limb weakness over six months, now unable to walk without a walking aid.
resident.history: Fifty-one-year-old delivery man with no significant past medical history presented with progressive unsteadiness and bilateral lower limb weakness over six months, worsening to inability to walk without a walking aid. He also had chronic neck stiffness for over two years and had not sought intervention. He denied any difficulty with hand dexterity, such as using chopsticks, buttoning a shirt, or picking up a coin.
resident.physical_exam: Neurological examination revealed signs of myelopathy in the lower limbs. MRC muscle power grading in both lower limbs (L2-S1) was 4/5. Deep tendon reflexes, including knee jerk and ankle jerk, were exaggerated bilaterally. Babinski's sign was positive bilaterally. The patient had difficulty getting up from an armless chair and was unable to perform tandem gait. No upper limb signs were demonstrated: sensory-motor function and reflexes were normal in both upper limbs, and Hoffman's sign was negative.
key_positive_signs: Exaggerated knee and ankle deep tendon reflexes bilaterally
Difficulty rising from an armless chair
resident.past_history: No significant past medical history. Chronic neck stiffness for over two years, for which he did not seek intervention.
resident.public_message: A 51-year-old man presented with six months of progressive unsteadiness and bilateral lower limb weakness, now requiring a walking aid, and chronic neck stiffness for over two years. Examination showed bilateral lower limb weakness (MRC 4/5), exaggerated knee and ankle reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, difficulty rising from a chair, and inability to tandem gait; upper limbs were neurologically normal. JOA score was 14/17 (grade 1 disability). Cervical spine X-rays showed degeneration with loss of lordosis and anterior osteophytes C3-C6; CT and MRI showed extensive OPLL from C3 to T3 causing significant canal compromise with no cord signal changes. Diagnosis: extensive cervicothoracic OPLL causing myelopathy.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record’s description only; the films were not available for review. CT and MRI were described as showing extensive ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) from C3-T3 with significant canal compromise. No cord signal change was reported. The direction of compression and a graded severity of stenosis were not stated. The described imaging has high correlation with the reported myelopathic symptoms.

neurology.localization: The examination localizes to an upper motor neuron lesion above the lumbosacral enlargement, consistent with myelopathy. Bilateral lower limb weakness with exaggerated knee and ankle reflexes, and positive Babinski signs indicate corticospinal tract dysfunction. The absence of upper limb motor, sensory, or reflex abnormalities and a negative Hoffman sign, together with no documented sensory level or sphincter disturbance, means the clinical level cannot be pinpointed to the cervical cord alone; it is compatible with lower cervical or upper thoracic cord involvement. The OPLL from C3 to T3 provides a structural correlate. Lower-limb-predominant myelopathy is well recognized in OPLL because the laterally placed lower-limb fibers in the corticospinal tract and the longest axons are most vulnerable to anterior compression. The examination is incomplete as lower limb sensory function, sensory level, and sphincter function are not documented.

red_flags.finding: Normal upper limb motor/sensory/reflexes and negative Hoffman despite OPLL from C3.
red_flags.rationale: Lower-limb-predominant myelopathy is common in OPLL because the lower-limb corticospinal fibers are more laterally placed and more vulnerable to anterior compression, and early disease often spares the upper limbs. This does not offer an alternative cause and does not change the levels already identified by imaging.

red_flags.finding: No cord T2 signal change on MRI.
red_flags.rationale: Absence of T2 hyperintensity does not exclude clinically significant myelopathy, especially in early or dynamic compression. It is not an alternative explanation and does not alter the indication; it may suggest less severe cord damage but does not change the plan.

red_flags.finding: Incomplete documentation of lower limb sensory exam, sensory level, and sphincter function.
red_flags.rationale: The missing data limit precise clinical localization and cannot confirm a sensory level matching the imaged OPLL. However, the upper motor neuron signs already establish a myelopathy above the lumbosacral enlargement, so this gap does not change the diagnosis or the surgical plan.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: There is no fundamental mismatch: the imaging shows extensive C3-T3 OPLL with canal compromise that can explain the bilateral lower limb upper motor neuron syndrome. Notable but non-contradictory observations are the absence of upper limb signs despite C3 involvement and absent cord signal change; both are consistent with early, leg-predominant cervical/thoracic myelopathy. The exact symptomatic level cannot be determined from the examination because lower limb sensory level and sphincter function were not documented.
neurology.public_message: The examination localizes to an upper motor neuron lesion above the lumbosacral enlargement, consistent with myelopathy; the absence of upper limb signs means the clinical level is likely lower cervical or upper thoracic, not definitively C3. The imaging shows extensive C3-T3 OPLL with canal compromise, which explains the dominant lower-limb syndrome; the symptom-imaging match is high. Notable findings are all coexisting and do not change the indication or plan: (1) normal upper limbs despite C3 involvement—common in early leg-predominant OPLL; (2) no cord T2 signal—does not exclude myelopathy; (3) incomplete sensory/sphincter documentation—limits precise level but not diagnosis. There is no evidence of coexisting peripheral neuropathy or central sensitization.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA grade III. Intraoperative MAP target 75 mmHg. Expected blood loss risk moderate. Prone position tolerance moderate. Extubation difficulty unassessable: no airway assessment on record.

preconditions_for_failure: Worsening of lower limb weakness or gait instability, such as new falls or inability to walk even with an aid
Development of new upper limb symptoms, sphincter dysfunction, or a drop in JOA score by 2 or more points
No stabilization or improvement of neurological status after 3 months of structured conservative treatment
Evidence of new or progressive cord signal change on follow-up MRI
physiatrist_opening.public_message: I acknowledge that progressive myelopathy carries a risk with delay. However, the absence of cord signal change on MRI and the relatively preserved JOA score (14/17) leave a narrow window for a time-limited, closely monitored conservative trial. A structured program of physical therapy, gait training, activity modification, and serial neurological assessments could be offered for 3-6 months, provided the patient is fully informed and there is immediate access to surgical evaluation if any failure criterion is met. This approach is not without risk, but surgery for extensive OPLL also carries significant morbidity, and early intervention may still be possible if deterioration occurs.

vice_opinions.assessment: This patient has progressive myelopathy from extensive C3-T3 OPLL with significant canal compromise. Despite normal upper limbs, no cord T2 signal, and JOA 14, the documented progression over six months and objective lower limb long-tract signs make this a surgical indication; watchful waiting risks irreversible deterioration. However, the imaging report alone is insufficient to select the exact surgical approach: the direction of compression (anterior vs circumferential), degree of stenosis at each level, spinal alignment, and presence of dural ossification are not documented. I would not endorse a 3-6 month conservative trial as first-line because myelopathy is already progressive; if any conservative option is considered, it should be only for very selected cases with fail criteria. My preferred option is early posterior decompression and instrumented fusion across the stenotic segments (likely C3-T3), with possible anterior supplementation if dominant anterior compression or kyphosis is confirmed on review of the actual images.
proposed_options: Posterior decompression and instrumented fusion (e.g., C3-T3 laminectomy or laminoplasty with fusion)
Anterior decompression with corpectomy/OPLL resection for dominant anterior compression if localized
Combined anterior-posterior decompression and fusion if severe kyphosis or circumferential compression
Structured conservative management with close monitoring and predefined surgical triggers (not my preferred first-line, but listed for completeness)
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior decompression and instrumented fusion across the stenotic segments (C3-T3), pending review of actual imaging and alignment.
disagreement_points: Whether any conservative trial can be justified despite progressive myelopathy; I believe the risk of irreversible cord damage outweighs the appeal of avoiding surgery, but the absence of cord signal change and preserved JOA score make this a contested point.

The exact surgical approach (posterior alone vs anterior vs combined) cannot be definitively chosen without reviewing the actual CT/MRI and determining the direction and severity of compression; I have stated my default posterior strategy, but this should be revised if the images show dominant anterior mass or kyphosis.

The fusion extent: whether to include the entire OPLL span C3-T3 or only the clinically relevant levels; including the full span may reduce adjacent-segment disease, but increases stiffness and operative morbidity.
The relevance of normal upper limbs despite C3 involvement raises uncertainty about the true clinical level; additional neurophysiology or imaging may be needed to localize.
deferred_questions_to_director: Do you agree that early surgery is indicated over a time-limited conservative trial in this progressive myelopathy?

Given the imaging is not available for our review, would you proceed with a default posterior decompression/fusion, or do you want additional imaging (CT myelogram, flexion-extension views, axial T2) before deciding?
What is your preferred fusion extent: the full OPLL segment C3-T3 or a shorter construct based on clinical and radiological stenosis?
If the images show predominant anterior compression or kyphosis, would you consider anterior or combined approach, and are you willing to involve a specialist who performs anterior OPLL resection?
vice_opinions.public_message: My professional judgement is that this is progressive OPLL myelopathy warranting early surgical decompression. I favour posterior decompression and instrumented fusion across the stenotic segments, but I have raised several contested points for the director's decision: whether any conservative trial can be justified, the precise surgical approach and fusion extent, and the need to review the actual imaging before finalising. I recommend obtaining the films and possibly a CT myelogram, and I defer the final decision to the director.

vice_opinions.assessment: Progressive myelopathy from extensive C3-T3 OPLL is a clear indication for surgical decompression. The absence of cord T2 signal and a JOA of 14 do not offset the documented six-month deterioration to cane use with objective corticospinal tract signs. I agree with the director that a conservative trial is not justified; the risk of irreversible cord injury outweighs operative morbidity. Final approach requires actual imaging: the default posterior decompression with instrumented fusion is reasonable for extensive posterior compression and preserved lordosis, but if imaging shows anterior-dominant compression or kyphosis, a combined or anterior approach may be safer. Fusion extent across the C3-T3 stenotic segment and choice of laminoplasty versus laminectomy-fusion remain unresolved.
proposed_options: Posterior decompression with instrumented fusion from C3 to T3 (or as dictated by stenotic segments) after confirming no significant kyphosis or anterior compression; this is my default.
Combined anterior-posterior approach or anterior decompression if imaging shows predominant ventral compression or kyphosis; this would be the contingency.

Cervical laminoplasty alone if lordosis is maintained and no instability, though I would not select this over fusion given OPLL extent and higher risk of post-operative kyphosis or inadequate decompression.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior decompression and instrumented fusion from C3 to T3 after reviewing the actual imaging and confirming no significant kyphosis or anterior-dominant compression; if either is present, switch to combined anterior-posterior decompression.
disagreement_points: I disagree with the physiatrist's conservative trial: progressive myelopathy with lower-limb weakness requiring a cane and positive Babinski is sufficient for surgery; no T2 signal is not reassuring, and delay risks irreversible cord damage.

The choice of surgery is not settled: posterior-only may be inadequate if the OPLL occupying ratio is high or if there is a component of anterior compression; we need the original films and the requested CT myelogram before finalising.
The extent of fusion and whether to cross the cervicothoracic junction remains contested; including T3 may be necessary but adds morbidity, and stopping short risks adjacent segment pathology.

Whether laminoplasty without fusion is an acceptable alternative is unresolved; I lean toward instrumented fusion to prevent post-laminectomy kyphosis, but this should be decided after flexion-extension views.
deferred_questions_to_director: After you review the imaging, what criteria will you use to switch from the default posterior approach to anterior/combined? For example, will you set a threshold for occupying ratio (>50-60%) or kyphosis (>10°)?
If posterior-only is confirmed, should we fuse the full C3-T3 stenotic segment or can we limit fusion to the levels of maximal compression and perform laminoplasty above/below?
Should we obtain preoperative neurophysiology (SSEP/MEP baseline) to help correlate the clinical level given the normal upper limbs despite C3 involvement?
vice_opinions.public_message: I agree with the director that this is progressive OPLL myelopathy and that a conservative trial is not appropriate. My preferred plan remains early posterior decompression with instrumented fusion across the stenotic segments, but the actual approach must await imaging. I have three open questions for the director: (1) What imaging findings would trigger an anterior or combined approach? (2) Should fusion extend to T3 or can we stop at T1? (3) Is there a role for laminoplasty alone? I request the radiologist's detailed review of the original CT/MRI and the new CT myelogram and flexion-extension films before we finalise.
